title: 2017 Steph Curry Shot Attribute Analysis
universal_lens: Body pose attributes as stochastic manifolds underlie NBA shooting mechanics, enabling probabilistic inference of shot success via phase-space trajectories. Temporal binning of basketball shooting actions enables a structured phase-space decomposition for probabilistic shot outcome modeling.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference of shot outcome conditioned on body pose attribute distributions using chi-squared test for statistical significance in made vs. missed shots. Bayesian inference on shot bin states allows dynamic belief updates over player intent and execution quality using conformal predictive distributions.
gse_mapping: Situational reasoning maps player body pose transitions through shot phases into state-transition graphs for real-time tactical adaptation and predictive modeling. Situation-aware state transitions between shot bins enable real-time tactical decision-making through stochastic control of player kinematics.

primitives.name: Body Pose Attribute Manifold
primitives.verbatim_quote: Body Shots": Analyzing Shooting Styles in the NBA using Body Pose Panna Felsen UC Berkeley and STATS panna@eecs.berkeley.edu Patrick Lucey STATS plucey@stats.com Abstract In this work we develop a novel attribute-based representation of a basketball player's body pose during his three point shot.
primitives.assumptions: Player body pose captured via 2D skeletal tracking; attributes represent kinematic features across shot execution phases.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When body pose data becomes unavailable or corrupted due to occlusion or sensor failure.

layer2.mapping: Each body pose attribute corresponds to a dimension in a latent manifold that encodes shooting style and mechanical consistency.
layer2.telemetry: Chi-squared distribution of attribute frequencies between made and missed shots.

primitives.name: Shot Phase Kinematic Space
primitives.verbatim_quote: The attributes are designed to capture the highlevel body movements of a player during the different phases of his shot, e.g., the jump and release.
primitives.assumptions: Shot execution can be segmented into discrete kinematic phases with distinct movement patterns.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When shot phase boundaries are ambiguous or mislabeled in video annotation.

layer2.mapping: Kinematic space derived from temporal sequences of body pose attributes to model dynamic behavior over time.
layer2.telemetry: Temporal variance in joint angles across shot phases.

primitives.name: Movement Style Distribution
primitives.verbatim_quote: Normalized for game context, we use Pearson's Chi-squaredtest toquantify differencesin attributedistributions for made and missed shots, where we observe statistically signi󰅭icant differences in distributions of attributes describing the style of movement, e.g., walk, run, or hop, in various phases of the shot.
primitives.assumptions: Statistical independence among movement styles; chi-squared test valid for categorical attribute comparison.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When sample size insufficient for reliable chi-squared estimation or when attribute categories are too sparse.

layer2.mapping: Distribution of movement styles forms a probability measure over the space of possible shooting postures.
layer2.telemetry: Observed frequency counts of movement types per shot outcome.

primitives.name: Curry Off-Balance Metric
primitives.verbatim_quote: We also present a case study for Stephen Curry, where we observe that Curry moves much more than the average player in all phases of his shot and he takes a higher proportion of off-balance shots compared to the average player.
primitives.assumptions: Off-balance shots correlate with increased shot difficulty; deviation from standard posture indicates risk factor.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When off-balance criteria are subjective or inconsistently applied across observers.

layer2.mapping: Computed deviation from baseline posture distribution to quantify off-balance tendency in elite shooters.
layer2.telemetry: Proportion of off-balance shots relative to total attempts per game.

primitives.name: Temporal Bin Structure
primitives.verbatim_quote: We divided the timeline of a shot into 󰅭ive bins: (blue) before the player possesses the ball, (pink) when the player possesses the ball before the shot, (black) immediately before the shot, (green) during the jump and release, and (red) after the player lands.
primitives.assumptions: Shot timeline is segmented into fixed discrete phases with deterministic transition boundaries.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Phase boundary ambiguity under high-speed motion or occlusion.

layer2.mapping: Each temporal bin maps to a conditional probability distribution over shot outcomes in GSI; GSE models transitions via Markovian state machines.
layer2.telemetry: Bin assignment accuracy from pose estimation algorithms.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 1 introduces a framework for analyzing basketball shooting through body pose attributes, leveraging advancements in computer vision to extract 2D skeletal data from broadcast footage. This approach addresses limitations of traditional SportVU trajectory data which lacks insight into specific motor skills like shooting form. By defining attributes that describe high-level body movements during shot execution—such as jump and release—the paper establishes a structured methodology for quantifying shooting mechanics. Using Pearson's chi-squared test, it demonstrates significant differences in attribute distributions between successful and unsuccessful shots, suggesting that movement style is predictive of outcome. The inclusion of a case study on Stephen Curry highlights how individual variation in movement patterns, particularly off-balance shooting, may contribute to elite performance. The theoretical foundation rests on the assumption that body pose encodes meaningful biomechanical information, enabling statistical modeling of shooting success. This aligns with broader trends in sports analytics where granular behavioral data enhances predictive models. The work contributes to the epistemology of athletic performance by proposing a formalism for capturing and interpreting human motion in complex environments. The shot attribute matrix further enriches this structure by encoding discrete variables such as balance, direction, footwork, and movement patterns. These attributes are essential for building predictive models that assess shot success probabilities. The integration of spatial and temporal features enables machine learning classifiers to learn complex relationships between player behavior and shooting outcomes. From a theoretical standpoint, this approach mirrors principles found in dynamical systems theory, where state transitions are governed by internal and external forces. reasoning_traces.think: Chapter window 3 (pages 6–8) introduces a methodological framework for analyzing basketball shooting through statistical inference over player attributes. The core idea is to compare attribute distributions across different shot classes using Pearson’s chi-squared test. This approach allows identification of which physical or behavioral attributes significantly differ between, e.g., tough vs. open shots, or made vs. missed shots. The framework operates under the assumption that contextual factors—such as game situation or shot outcome—produce measurable differences in player behavior. These differences are encoded in attribute histograms, which are then compared using statistical tests. The resulting p-values indicate whether such differences are statistically significant at α=0.1. The paper emphasizes that multiple attributes show significant variation across shot types, suggesting that player behavior is context-sensitive. This supports a Bayesian interpretation where prior knowledge about shot context informs posterior beliefs about player actions. From a GSE perspective, these comparisons form the basis for modeling situational reasoning—predicting what kind of shot a player might take given current game state. Meanwhile, GSI leverages these findings to construct probabilistic models of shot outcomes by treating attributes as latent variables. The use of chi-squared tests ensures robustness against noise while maintaining interpretability. The empirical validation comes from visualizing attribute distributions in Figures 3 and 4, which confirm that certain attributes (e.g., direction, footwork, landing foot) vary meaningfully across shot types. This supports the notion that player behavior is not random but structured according to game dynamics. The framework thus bridges descriptive statistics with predictive modeling, enabling both GSE and GSI to operationalize complex behavioral signals into actionable intelligence.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 4 explores the kinematic and behavioral attributes of Stephen Curry’s three-point shooting, focusing on how his shot style deviates from the norm. The core thesis is that Curry’s shooting is characterized by a higher frequency of off-balance and off-dribble shots, which correlates with increased motion and instability. This is supported by empirical data showing that these attributes are more prevalent in Curry’s shot repertoire compared to other players. The analysis further reveals that such attributes are not random but are part of a strategic pattern—Curry’s shots are more likely to be made when he is in motion, suggesting a dynamic control mechanism rather than static positioning. The freezing phenomenon after tough made shots indicates a psychological or physiological response to high-pressure situations, which is absent in open shots. This implies that Curry’s performance is not only governed by physical mechanics but also by mental resilience and adaptive behavior. The data suggests that Curry’s shooting style can be modeled as a stochastic process with non-linear feedback loops, where motion and timing are key variables. These insights form the basis for constructing a Bayesian belief network in GSI to predict shot outcomes and a state-transition model in GSE to simulate real-time decision-making.
